claims.text: The target material is an as-processed, multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct coexisting phases.
A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy can form a protective oxide scale during elevated-temperature exposure.
At high temperature, a protective oxide initially forms preferentially on the more corrosion-resistant phase.
High-temperature tribo-oxidation can produce an oxide glaze layer that protects a worn surface and provides solid lubrication.
Mechanical wear repeatedly ruptures the protective oxide film.
Compromise or breach of a protective oxide or coating permits localized chloride-driven corrosion.
The coexisting eutectic phases have galvanic potential differences.
Interphase boundaries exhibit differential oxide formation.
Interphase boundaries promote localized breakdown of protective oxide scales.
After oxide rupture, galvanic coupling between dissimilar eutectic phases intensifies localized corrosion at interphase boundaries.
Cyclic oxide disruption followed by localized galvanic attack is the primary driver of accelerated coupled degradation.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will cause total degradation greater than the sum of degradation measured during isolated wear and isolated corrosion.
Corrosion-assisted removal or loss of the protective oxide will increase wear relative to isolated wear.
Wear-induced exposure of interphase boundaries will increase corrosion relative to isolated corrosion.
The simultaneous condition will produce greater mass loss, surface roughness, and pit formation than the additive isolated responses.
Exposure near 800 degrees Celsius can accelerate corrosion in material exposed to 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
The proposed mechanism applies under approximately 800 degrees Celsius, corrosive exposure, and mechanical loading.
Lower temperatures or alternative corrosive media could change the interaction between wear and corrosion.
The magnitude of the coupled degradation increase depends on alloy composition, microstructural heterogeneity, and wear conditions.

contradictions.description: The baseline requires an isolated-wear test under the same environmental conditions as the simultaneous test, while those conditions include a corrosive medium. If the corrosive medium remains present, the test is not wear-only; if it is removed, the environmental conditions are not identical. The design must distinguish controlled thermal/mechanical matching from presence or absence of the corrosive exposure.
